# Mobile apps: where to start

How screens are kept from becoming god objects, how state survives lifecycle and flaky networks, and what an app shipped to devices you can't update may hold or assume.

Flags: **C** contested (offer it as a choice, with both sides) · **A** agents do this readily · **T** has a one-file tell · **E** has a pseudo-code example.

Axes in brackets: ⊕ the lens's primary effect, the reason to reach for it · + also helps · − costs. Laws name the axes they bear on. See [AXES.md](../AXES.md).

`{kinds}`: where it matters most. `langs:` which languages have notes. `→` related lenses.

## Probes for the interview

Find first, in the code, docs, git history, CI and config. Ask only what the repository can't tell, in the project's own terms, with the evidence and a recommendation. Skip the question when the findings settle it. Also see the general stances in [THINKING.md](../THINKING.md).

### 1. Breaking-Change Surface, Deprecation Policy

**Find:** Minimum supported OS versions, any forced-update mechanism, how the API is versioned, version checks in the app and code on the backend (if in reach) that still handles old clients. Release history and its cadence. Docs on support windows.

**Ask:** "The app <has / has no> forced update, the API <is versioned by X>, and <code> still handles clients older than <version>. How long must old versions keep working? I'd <set a window of N releases or months and force-update past it> because <reason>."

**Settled when:** A support window is written down and the code matches it. The agent cites it and asks whether it holds. Which versions are actually installed is never in the repo.

### 2. Ninety-ninety rule

**Find:** For features merged in the last year or so: later commits or pull requests that reference the same issue or pull request, or touch the same files within a few weeks with a fix-style message. Sort them by cause: lifecycle and background states, offline handling, screen sizes and devices, accessibility, store review. Any PR template or definition-of-done checklist.

**Ask:** "Follow-up fixes after features were mostly about <category> (<examples>). I'd make <X> part of every feature from its first commit, because <reason>. Is that the tail that holds features up for you?"

**Settled when:** A checklist already covers the categories the history shows. The agent confirms it.

### 3. Production Bugs, Murphy's law

**Find:** Fix commits and linked crash or bug reports, sorted by cause (lifecycle, process death, network loss, rotation, permissions). Whether any test creates those states: backgrounding, restore after process death, offline, slow network.

**Ask:** "<k> of the last <N> fixes came from <lifecycle / network> states (<examples>), and no test creates <them>. Were there others that reached users? I'd add <tests for X> to every screen that <condition>, because <reason>."

**Settled when:** Never fully: which bugs reached users isn't in the repo. With linked crash reports the ask shrinks to confirming the pattern.

### 4. The Hype Cycle & Amara's Law

**Find:** Counts of screens per UI toolkit and per concurrency model (old and new side by side), the direction over time, and what screens added in the last months use. Migration notes.

**Ask:** "<N> screens use <old>, <M> use <new>, and every screen added since <date> uses <new>. I'd have new screens use <new>, and move an old screen only when it needs real work, because <reason>. Right?"

**Settled when:** There's no migration, or all new screens already use the new side and a doc says so. The agent confirms it.
